ver.etymology: From Latin vērus (“true”), from Proto-Italic *wēros, from a Proto-Indo-European *weh₁-ros, from *weh₁- (“true”).

set.etymology: From Latin septem, from Proto-Italic *septem. Cognates include Italian sette and French sept.

un.etymology: Inherited from Latin ūnus, from Old Latin oinos, from Proto-Italic *oinos. Cognates include Italian uno and French un.

tre.etymology: From Latin trēs, from Proto-Italic *trēs. Cognates include Italian tre and French trois.

ca.etymology: Inherited from Latin casa. Compare Italian casa, Lombard cà.

union.etymology: Borrowed from Late Latin ūniō, ūniōnem (“oneness, unity”), from Latin ūnus (“one”).

glosses_en: Turin (a city and comune, the capital of the Metropolitan City of Turin and the region of Piedmont, Italy)
Turin (a metropolitan city of Piedmont, established in 2015; in full, the Metropolitan City of Turin)
Turin.etymology: From Latin Augusta Taurinōrum, ultimately from the name of the Taurini tribe.

vita.etymology: From Latin vīta, from Proto-Italic *gʷītā, possibly a derivative of Proto-Indo-European *gʷih₃wo-teh₂, from the root *gʷeyh₃- (“to live”).

neu.etymology: Inherited from Latin nōdus, from Proto-Indo-European *gned-, *gnod- (“to bind”).

esse.etymology: Inherited from Early Medieval Latin essere, from Latin esse.

montagna.etymology: Inherited from Early Medieval Latin montānia, a collective based on Latin montem.

dent.etymology: From Latin dēns, dentem, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃dénts, *h₃dónts.

trist.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin trīstus, from Latin trīstis. Compare Italian tristo.

des.etymology: From Latin decem, from Proto-Italic *dekem. Cognates include Italian diece and French dix.

pais.etymology: Inherited from Late Latin pāgēnsis. Compare Italian paese, French pays

tut.etymology: From Vulgar Latin tōttus, alteration of Latin tōtus.

argent.etymology:
Ultimately inherited from Latin argentum n.
Compare cognates Occitan argent m, Catalan argent m, Friulian arint m, Lombard arsgent, Italian argento m, and French argent m.

bosch.etymology: Inherited from Early Medieval Latin boscus, borrowed from Frankish *busk, from Proto-Germanic *buskaz.

passé.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *passāre, derived from Latin passus (“step”, noun).

ses.etymology: From Latin sex, from Proto-Italic *seks. Cognates include Italian sei and French six.

venial.etymology: From Late Latin veniālis (“pardonable”) (probably via Italian veniale), from Latin venia (“forgiveness”).

prima.etymology: From Late Latin prīma vēra (“early spring”).

tragedia.etymology: From Latin tragoedia, from Ancient Greek τρᾰγῳδῐ́ᾱ (trăgōidĭ́ā), from τρᾰ́γος (trắgos, “male goat”) + ᾠδή (ōidḗ, “song”).

eut.etymology: From Latin octō, from Proto-Italic *oktō. Cognates include Italian otto and French huit.

strut.etymology: From the past participle of dëstrue (“to melt, destroy”), from Vulgar Latin *destrugo (“I destroy”).

doi.etymology: From Latin duo, from Proto-Italic *duō. Cognates include Italian due and Spanish dos.

luv.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *lūpum, from Latin lŭpum.

mur.etymology: From Latin mūrum, accusative singular of mūrus.

metan.etymology: From French méthane and German Methan.

eva.etymology: Inherited from Old Piedmontese aigua, aiva, from Latin aqua. Compare French eau, Romansh ava, ova.

glosses_en: bagna cauda (dip made from anchovies, olive oil and garlic)

stival.etymology: Often derived from a Late Latin aestivalis (“summer”).

andè.etymology: From Early Medieval Latin andāre, of uncertain origin.

vorej.etymology: From Vulgar Latin volēre, regularized from Latin velle.

mondan.etymology: From Late Latin mundānus. Compare French mondain.

tajé.etymology: From Late Latin tāliāre, a verb based on Latin tālea (“cutting taken from a plant”).

velen.etymology: Ultimately from Latin venēnum. In this form, perhaps borrowed from Italian veleno.

fermé.etymology: From Latin firmō (“to confirm, make firm”).

quaranta.etymology: From Late Latin quarranta, from Latin quadraginta (“forty”), q.v.

foresta.etymology: Derived from Early Medieval Latin foresta.

limon.etymology: (This etymology is missing or incomplete. Please add to it, or discuss it at the Etymology scriptorium. )

glosses_en: vice versa, the other way round

lenga.etymology: From Latin lingua, from Old Latin dingua, from Proto-Italic *dn̥ɣwā, from Proto-Indo-European *dn̥ǵʰwéh₂s.

fiorì.etymology: From Late Latin flōrīre, from Latin flōrēre.

glosses_en: Transnistria (a geographic region and de-facto independent but unrecognized country in Eastern Europe that claims statehood as the Pridnestrovian Moldavian Republic; internationally considered an autonomous territorial unit within Moldova)

mineur.etymology:
Borrowing from French mineur.
The inherited form is mënào

glosses_en: curtain (woven fabric to cover, e.g., windows)

giova.etymology: Ultimately from Vulgar Latin *ga(v)ota. Perhaps a recent borrowing from French joue.

velenos.etymology: From Late Latin venēnōsus, from Latin venēnum.

ceia.etymology: Inherited from Early Medieval Latin clēta.

neuit.etymology:
Etymology tree
Proto-Indo-European *nókʷts
Proto-Italic *nok⁽ʷ⁾ts
Latin nox
Piedmontese neuit
Inherited from Latin nox, from Proto-Italic *nok⁽ʷ⁾ts, from Proto-Indo-European *nókʷts.

verd.etymology: From Late Latin virdis, from Latin viridis, viridem.

anciova.etymology: From Ligurian anciôa, from Vulgar Latin *apiuva, from Latin aphyē (“small fry”), from Ancient Greek ἀφύη (aphúē).

rava.etymology: From Latin rāpa, neuter plural of rāpum, reinterpreted as a feminine singular.

glosses_en: to be at ease, to have time

cadrega.etymology: From Vulgar Latin cathégra (attested in Pompeiian inscriptions), variant of Latin cathedra (“seat”), from Ancient Greek κᾰθέδρᾱ (kăthédrā, “chair of a teacher, throne”), from κᾰτᾰ́ (kătắ, “down”) + ἕδρᾱ (hédrā, “seat”). Compare Lombard cadr

scòla.etymology: From Latin schola (“school”), from Ancient Greek σχολή (skholḗ).

glosses_en: mister, sir (a title or form of address for a man)
monsù.etymology: From French monsieur, from mon (“my”) + sieur (“sir”). Second element is from the oblique case of Old French sire, ultimately from Latin senior (“older, elder”)}}.

rusca.etymology:
Etymology tree
Proto-Indo-European *Hrew-der.
Proto-Indo-European *h₃rewk-
Proto-Celtic *rukskos
Proto-Celtic *rūskos
Gaulish rūscabor.
Early Medieval Latin rusca
Piedmontese rusca
Inherited from Early Medieval Latin rusca (“bark”), borrowe

poj.etymology: From French pou (“louse”), from Latin pedīculus (“louse”).

piat.etymology: From Italian piatto (“dish”), from Vulgar Latin *plattus, from Ancient Greek πλατύς (platús, “broad, flat”).

glosses_en: Piedmont (an administrative region in the north of Italy)

avèj.etymology: From an older aveir from Latin habeō.

glosses_en: A terracotta pot, with a space underneath for a heater, used to make bagna cauda or fonduta.

neuse.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *nocĕre, from Latin nocēre.

glosses_en: A sort of rounded cake mold.
A traditional Piedmontese pudding prepared with cocoa and amaretti.
bonet.etymology: Borrowed from Middle French bonet (Modern French bonnet), from Old French bonet (“material from which hats are made”), from Frankish *bunni (“that which is bound”), from Proto-Germanic *bundiją (“bundle”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰendʰ-

bondon.etymology: Ultimately from Gaulish *bunda, feminine form of *bundos (“bottom”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰudʰ-, *bʰudʰmḗn. Cognate with French bondon.

glosses_en: a male given name, equivalent to English Jair
Giairo.etymology: From Latin Iaīrus, from Ancient Greek Ἰάϊρος (Iáïros), from Biblical Hebrew יָאִיר (Ya'ir).

Pininfarina.etymology: pinin + Farina. From the founder patriarch of the Pininfarina family, who was the youngest brother (pinin) of a family named Farina.

glosses_en: Genoa (a port city and comune, the capital of the Metropolitan City of Genoa and the region of Liguria, Italy)
Genoa (a metropolitan city of Liguria, established in 2015; in full, the Metropolitan City of Genoa)
A type of it that is thicker than capellini, traditionally served with meat sauces; a dish of Langhe and Montferrat.
tajarin.etymology: From the root of tajé (“to cut”) + -in (noun-forming diminutive suffix).

volté.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *vol(vi)tāre, derived from Latin volvere.

vardé.etymology: Inherited from Early Medieval Latin wardāre.

travajé.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *tripāliāre (“torment”), from Late Latin tripālium (“torture device”).

tràfich.etymology:
Of uncertain origin, possibilities including:
* From Catalan trafegar (“to decant”)
* From a derivative of Latin trans- + Italian ficcare (“to thrust in”)
* From Vulgar Latin *trānsfrīcō (“to rub across”), from trans- + frico
* From Arabic

primièr.etymology: From Latin prīmārius. Replaced by prim or prum, borrowed from Italian primo.

milsa.etymology: From Lombardic or Old High German milza, from Proto-West Germanic *miltijā, *meltā, from Proto-Germanic *meltǭ. Cognate with German Milz, English milt.

zòna.etymology: From Latin zōna, from Ancient Greek ζώνη (zṓnē).

làit.etymology: From Late Latin lactem, from Latin lac.

quatr.etymology: From Latin quattuor, from Proto-Italic *kʷettwōr. Cognates include Italian quattro and French quatre.

neuv.etymology: Inherited from Latin novem, from Proto-Italic *nowem. Cognates include Italian nove and French neuf.

giaj.etymology: From Latin gagāten, accusative singular of gagātes (“jet”), from Ancient Greek Γαγάτης (Gagátēs, “lignite; jet; literally ‘stone of Gagas’”).

euv.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin (*)ŏvum, from Classical Latin ōvum.

glosses_en: to exhaust, to make utterly tired

sufrì.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *sufferīre, from Latin sufferre.

rusié.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *rōsicāre, frequentative based on Latin rōdere (“gnaw”).

miraj.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *mīrāculum (“mirror”), a noun based on Latin mīrārī (“gaze at”).

apress.etymology: From Late Latin ad pressum, from Latin ad + pressum.

manoscrit.etymology: From Latin manū scrīptus, manū scrīptum (literally “written by hand”).

bianch.etymology: From Early Medieval Latin blancus, from Frankish. Compare Italian bianco.

ciav.etymology: From Latin clavis. Compare Portuguese chave and Venetan ciave.

Giapon.etymology: From French Japon, from Malay Jepang, from Hokkien 日本 (Ji̍t-pún), from Middle Chinese 日本 (nyit pwon^X). Compare Italian Giappone, Lombard Gjapon.

còrp.etymology: From Latin corpus ("body"). Compare to Lombard còrp, Italian corpo, Spanish cuerpo, Catalan cos, French corps, Romanian corp, Friulian cuarp.

glosses_en: Jamaica (an island and country in the Caribbean)

pich.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *piccus (“peak, sharp point, pike”)

frèid.etymology: From Latin frīgidus (“cold”) (through a syncopated Vulgar Latin or Late Latin form frigdus, fricdus, attested in the Appendix Probi, or fridus, on a Pompeian inscription).

glosses_en: A Turinese beverage made of espresso, hot chocolate, and milk.
bicerin.etymology: From bicer (“glass, cup”) + -in (diminutive suffix). Compare Italian bicchierino.

glosses_en: Autonomous region of Italy situated in the Alps. See Valle d'Aosta

figlol.etymology: From Latin filiolus, diminutive from fīlius (“son”) + -olus.

glosses_en: bilberry, whortleberry, blueberry, bearberry, cranberry, lingonberry, cowberry, huckleberry; a plant of the genus Vaccinium
a fruit of a plant of the genus Vaccinium

giassa.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *glacium/a, from Latin glaciēs.

ancheuj.etymology: Compare Ligurian ancheu, Italian ancoi, Venetan ancoi, Ladin ncuei

guèra.etymology: Inherited from Early Medieval Latin werra. Compare Italian guerra, Venetan guèra.

bunza.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *buttia. Compare Sicilian bonza.

glosses_en: to arrange, to set up, to organize

nojé.etymology: Ultimately from Late Latin inodiāre, perhaps via Old French enoiier. Compare Italian annoiare.

glosses_en: a male given name, equivalent to English John.
